Gubernatorial is an adjective that means relating to a governor or to the office and role of a governor.

Think of it this way: just as "presidential" means "relating to a president," gubernatorial means "relating to a governor." It is simply the adjective form of the word "governor."

A governor is the elected head of a state or province — the top political leader at the state level (as opposed to the national level). In the United States, each of the 50 states has its own governor. Think of a governor as the "president of a state."

The word is used to describe anything that belongs to, involves, or connects to a governor's world — their election, their powers, their duties, their term in office, and so on. Here are the most common combinations:

A gubernatorial election / race / campaign — an election held to choose a governor.

A gubernatorial candidate — a person running to become a governor.

A gubernatorial debate — a formal debate between people competing for the governorship.

A gubernatorial term — the fixed period of time a governor serves in office (commonly four years).

A gubernatorial appointment — a decision by a governor to assign a specific person to an official position or role.

Gubernatorial duties / responsibilities — the everyday tasks and functions a governor is expected to carry out.

Gubernatorial authority / power — the legal power that comes with holding the office of governor.

A gubernatorial veto — when a governor officially rejects or blocks a bill passed by the state legislature.

• "The gubernatorial election in Texas attracted millions of voters."
  • "She announced her gubernatorial campaign on Monday."
  • "He used his gubernatorial authority to pardon the prisoner."
  • "The two candidates clashed fiercely in the gubernatorial debate."
  • "His gubernatorial term lasted four years before he stepped down."
  • "The new policy was one of her most controversial gubernatorial decisions."

Gubernatorial does not simply refer to a governor as a person — it refers to the office, role, and function of a governor. So "gubernatorial power" means the power that is attached to the position of governor, not the personal strength of one individual. This distinction matters in legal and political writing, where precision is essential.

This is a formal word. You will encounter it almost exclusively in news articles, legal documents, political speeches, and official reports. In everyday casual speech, people tend to say "the governor's race" or "the governor's powers" instead. However, the moment writing becomes formal — especially in journalism — "gubernatorial" is the precise and preferred term.
Can it be used outside the United States?

Yes. While gubernatorial is most common in American English (because the U.S. has a well-established, prominent governor system), it can technically apply to any governor-like figure anywhere in the world. Any region or country that has a political office called a "governorship" can use this word.
If you ever see the word gubernatorial, simply ask yourself: "Does this have something to do with a governor or their office?" If the answer is yes, you understand the word completely.
